analysis.one_liner: Makes hardrock mining companies pay royalties, fees, and cleanup bonds for extracting minerals from public land.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a single hearing vote or floor vote: it was referred to the House Resources Committee on May 15, 2003, sent to a subcommittee six days later, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Mining Law of 1872, anyone can stake a claim on federal land and take hardrock minerals like gold and copper without paying the government a royalty, and can buy the land outright for as little as a few dollars an acre. This bill would have charged mining companies an 8 percent royalty on what they take, a $100 annual fee per claim, and a $25 fee per new claim, and would have required companies to post cleanup bonds and meet reclamation standards before disturbing public land. The money would have gone into a fund to clean up the hundreds of thousands of abandoned hardrock mines that pollute streams across the West. The bill also would have barred new mining claims in wilderness study areas, wild and scenic river corridors, and other protected lands.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently get nothing for minerals taken from land they own; communities downstream of abandoned mines, whose water would have benefited from the new cleanup fund; and outdoor users of public lands, who would have gained stronger protections from mine disturbance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Charges an 8 percent royalty on the value of locatable minerals produced from federal mining claims, money the government currently does not collect under the 1872 Mining Law.

Replaces the nominal annual claim-maintenance requirement with a $100-per-claim fee and adds a $25 location fee on new claims, with all revenue deposited into a new Abandoned Locatable Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund for cleanup of abandoned hardrock mines.

Requires an operations permit for any mining activity beyond casual use, along with reclamation standards, a full reclamation plan, and financial assurance (a bond or equivalent) large enough to cover the cost of reclaiming the site and treating contaminated water even if the operator walks away.
Denies permits to companies or their affiliates with unresolved environmental violations and requires public notice, comment, and the chance for a hearing before any permit is approved.
Effectively ends new patents, the conversion of mining claims into outright private ownership of federal land, by limiting patents to claims with applications filed before September 30, 1994.
Closes wilderness study areas, recommended wilderness, wild and scenic river corridors, Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, and identified sacred sites to new mining claims.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, which would owe royalties, annual fees, permit application fees, and cleanup bonds covering the full projected cost of reclamation and water treatment. Some of that cost would likely be passed on through higher mineral prices, and some marginal projects might not go forward.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: The 8 percent royalty and full reclamation bonds would raise operating costs on federal land, which could reduce domestic hardrock production and mining jobs in rural Western communities, and industry argued the royalty would push exploration overseas.

The permitting regime is heavy: applicants must produce hydrologic analyses, biological surveys, accident contingency plans, and proof the deposit is economically viable after compliance costs, which adds time and expense, particularly for smaller operators.

The bill does include a break for the smallest claim holders: those with ten or fewer claims may continue doing annual assessment work instead of paying the $100 fee, but anyone with more than ten claims pays in full.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit side is large and concrete: an end to royalty-free extraction of publicly owned minerals and a dedicated funding stream for cleaning up abandoned mines, which are a major ongoing source of water pollution in the West. The costs fall on a specific, profitable industry and would partly show up in mineral prices or forgone marginal projects. The cleanup fund, permit process, and bond requirement are modeled on rules that already apply to coal mining on federal land, so the design was not experimental. The main honest objection is economic: some marginal mines would not pencil out under these costs, and mining towns would feel that.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Resources Committee, which passed it down to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Rahall of West Virginia introduced the bill on May 15, 2003, joined by 21 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 1 Republican.
The House referred it to the Committee on Resources the same day and to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on May 21, 2003.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, they continued extracting gold, copper, and other minerals from federal land without paying royalties or posting full-cost cleanup bonds under the 1872 law, and taxpayers continued to bear the cost of abandoned mine pollution.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-WV); ranking member of the House Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on May 15, 2003.

against.name: House Resources Committee leadership (Chair Richard Pombo)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on May 21, 2003, and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the 108th Congress.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.what_they_did: The mining industry has long opposed royalties and reclamation bonding on federal hardrock claims, arguing they would cost jobs and drive exploration abroad.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were House members: 20 Democrats and just 1 Republican, and the Republican-controlled Resources Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining (gold, silver, copper and other locatable minerals)
industries.note: The bill would end the industry's century-old free ride on federal land: an 8 percent royalty, $100 annual claim fees, $25 location fees, permit fees, and cleanup bonds covering full reclamation and water-treatment costs. Its gain under the status quo comes at the public's expense, since taxpayers fund abandoned mine cleanup and receive nothing for minerals taken from public land.

industries.industry: Small mining claim holders (10 or fewer claims)
industries.note: Claimants with ten or fewer claims producing under $800,000 a year can keep doing annual assessment work instead of paying the $100 fee, but all claim holders still face the new permitting, reclamation, and bonding requirements.
The bill requires financial assurance in the form of surety bonds, trust funds, letters of credit, or equivalents before any operations permit is issued, creating demand for reclamation bonding.
